Opening

LAUNCH · RE & World Views · Autumn 1 · Week 2

Key beliefs across two worldviews

Learning goal

Identify a key belief in two worldviews and explain one similarity or difference.

How do beliefs and worldviews shape identity, values and choices?

I can explain an influence, compare two worldviews, identify a source of authority and give a structured explanation.

40 minutes, with flexible pauses. Point, speak, draw, type or write. A fictional example is welcome. Nobody is asked to share a personal belief.

Editable Word packPrintable pupil resources PDF

This is learning about religion and worldviews, not worship. Nobody is asked to share a personal belief, family detail or loss.

Arrival task

Previous lesson reminder:

Start with 1 and 2. Continue with 3 and 4 when ready.

1. How does Daniel’s belief influence his choice of work?

Help

Use the reminder strip or talk it through with an adult.

He believes everyone deserves dignity, so he chose care work.

2. Which meaning fits theist?

Help

Choose: A person who believes in God or gods OR Not following a religion, but still holding beliefs and values.

A person who believes in God or gods

3. Name one belief from each worldview.

Help

Use the model evidence anchor A, B or read one relevant card together.

For example: Christians believe in God as Trinity; Humanists believe this is our only life.

4. Do all Christians believe exactly the same things?

Help

Give a reason when ready.

No. Use “some”, “many” or “most”.

Word and evidence bank

A Christianity: key beliefs

Christians believe in one God, understood as Trinity. They believe Jesus is the Son of God, and that his teaching and example show how to live. Most believe in life after death.

Authored RE summary

Limit: Christians differ on many details.

B Humanism: key beliefs

Humanists do not believe in a god. They hold that this life is the only one we have, that reason and evidence are the best guides, and that people can live good lives without religion.

Authored summary of Humanists UK’s description of Humanism

Limit: Humanists differ on many details.

C Belief or practice?

A belief is held to be true: “God exists.” A practice is done: “going to church”. Compare belief with belief.

Authored classroom resource

Limit: Some statements mix both.

D Shared ground

Both worldviews value kindness, honesty and responsibility for others. They differ on God and on life after death.

Authored classroom resource

Limit: Sharing values does not make two worldviews the same.

LAUNCH · RE & World Views · Autumn 1 · Week 2

Independent application

Choose one route and one response mode. Keep the same learning goal.

Supported task

  1. Use the two-source set with symbols.
  2. Choose one belief from each worldview.

Use the glossary and one chunk of evidence. Plan the claim and supporting detail before explaining. Complete the organiser one space at a time. Both ___. However, Christians believe ___, whereas Humanists believe ___.

An adult may read or scribe your exact response. They should not choose the answer.

Stretch task

  1. Explain one similarity and one difference.
  2. Quote or paraphrase a card as evidence.
  3. Explain one consequence of the difference for daily life.

Choose the evidence independently. Use the frame only if it helps.

Knowledge organiser

Key beliefs across two worldviews

Learning goal: Identify a key belief in two worldviews and explain one similarity or difference.

Words to use

WordMeaning
theistA person who believes in God or gods
non-religiousNot following a religion, but still holding beliefs and values
HumanismA non-religious worldview based on reason, evidence and care for others
TrinityThe Christian belief in one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit

Remember

Name one belief from each worldview. For example: Christians believe in God as Trinity; Humanists believe this is our only life.

Do all Christians believe exactly the same things? No. Use “some”, “many” or “most”.

How to show your learning

Choose one similarity or one difference.

Both ___. However, Christians believe ___, whereas Humanists believe ___.

Evidence matters

Fictional cases are teaching examples. Historical, geographical and religious claims use the named sources. A model video demonstrates a method.

This is learning about religion and worldviews, not worship. Nobody is asked to share a personal belief, family detail or loss.

Sources: Humanists UK explanation of Humanism

Teacher brief

Teacher notes and answers

Teacher card

Key beliefs across two worldviews / LAUNCH_RE_A1_W02

Outcome: Identify a key belief in two worldviews and explain one similarity or difference.

Evidence to retain: F: one similarity or difference explained with evidence.

Forty minute route

Arrival 4 min; starter 3; model 6; shared task 7; check 2; independent 12; review 3; exit 3. Pause time is flexible.

Preparation

Choose one independent route. Print the evidence and shared cards, required visual or data sheet, route worksheet and exit. The organiser is one separate A4 page. Keep answers with staff.

Pre-teach vocabulary; avoid overgeneralising with ‘all’; . model 'some/many/this person’; check comprehension before comparison.

Access and regulation

Reduced two-source set; visual symbols; colour-coded similarities/differences; sentence frames; adult reading; verbal response accepted.

Offer a predictable start, private response and agreed pause. No cold calling or forced personal disclosure. Rejoin at one clearly named next step. Keep teen-appropriate examples and the same learning goal across response modes.

This is learning about religion and worldviews, not worship. Nobody is asked to share a personal belief, family detail or loss.

Assessment

Use questioning and the exit response to decide the next step. Record the learner’s individual contribution and the access support used.

UAS: no approved unit code is supplied. Match the learner’s evidence to the centre-selected unit and exact criteria before submission. This pack makes no automatic award claim.

Model and answers

Read these pages before teaching. Hide the model during independent assessment.

Question: Name one belief from each worldview.

Evidence: A Christianity: key beliefs: Christians believe in one God, understood as Trinity. They believe Jesus is the Son of God, and that his teaching and example show how to live. Most believe in life after death. B Humanism: key beliefs: Humanists do not believe in a god. They hold that this life is the only one we have, that reason and evidence are the best guides, and that people can live good lives without religion.

Think aloud: For example: Christians believe in God as Trinity; Humanists believe this is our only life.

Check: Do all Christians believe exactly the same things? No. Use “some”, “many” or “most”.

Arrival answers

1. He believes everyone deserves dignity, so he chose care work.

2. A person who believes in God or gods

3. For example: Christians believe in God as Trinity; Humanists believe this is our only life.

4. No. Use “some”, “many” or “most”.

Shared activity reasoning

1. God exists as Trinity — Christianity. Card A.

2. This life is the only one we have — Humanism. Card B.

3. People should care for others — Both. Cards A, B and D.

Exit responses

Name one belief from each worldview. For example: Christians believe in God as Trinity; Humanists believe this is our only life.

Do all Christians believe exactly the same things? No. Use “some”, “many” or “most”.

Teaching and evidence record

Supplied scheme of work teaching sequence: Arrival: 4 retrieval questions from Week 1. Starter: belief or practice? quick sort. I Do: introduce two accessible worldviews through short sources. We Do: complete a same/different comparison using belief cards. You Do: choose one similarity or difference and explain it with evidence. Exit ticket: name one belief from each worldview.

Look for

F: one similarity or difference explained with evidence.

Accept accurate equivalents, including speech or exact scribing. Check the concept and use of evidence rather than length or handwriting. Record access support separately from content prompting.

BUILD: a concrete example with a reason or demonstrated action. GROW: explain or compare with a relevant detail. LAUNCH: connect evidence and reasoning; use a limitation when the outcome requires it. Keep RE responses non-GCSE.

Media

Original captioned teaching model made for this pack. It demonstrates the supplied reasoning; it is not historical footage, survivor testimony or a documentary. The full transcript and factual source credits are included.

Use manual steps for a calm pace. The silent MP4 has visible captions and a matching text transcript. External archive media is optional and should be previewed before class.
